competitors.name: Free printable PDFs from parenting blogs (Chica and Jo, Wonder Mom Wannabe, Modern Mom Life, The Incremental Mama, Free Organizing Printables, The Homes I Have Made)
competitors.model: Free, ad-supported or email-gated; download a PDF or an editable Word doc
competitors.note: THIS is the real competitor. Google 'babysitter information sheet' and the entire first page is these. They are genuinely good at field coverage and they cost nothing. Weakness: you re-handwrite everything every single time (their own advice is to laminate it and use a dry-erase marker), the design is Pinterest-pretty rather than readable at a glance, and you need a printer.

competitors.name: Etsy / TPT / DesignBundles editable templates and nanny binders
competitors.model: Paid one-time, roughly $3-12; some 50+ page 'nanny binder' bundles
competitors.note: Sold as Canva templates or fillable PDFs. Listings state plainly 'You will need a free Canva account' — so a third-party signup is mandatory. Etsy's own Technical Issues forum is full of sellers reporting buyers who cannot download in the Etsy app or whose 'digital PDF files won't print,' and who leave 1-star reviews rather than contact the seller.

competitors.name: Sittercity / Care.com free template + checklist content
competitors.model: Free content marketing; the underlying marketplace is subscription
competitors.note: Sittercity's 'New Babysitter Information Guide (Free Template)' and Care.com's emergency-contact guides rank extremely well. They are lead magnets into a paid sitter marketplace, not tools. The advice quality is high and worth mining for field taxonomy; the artifact you get is still a static doc.

competitors.name: Cozi Family Organizer
competitors.model: Freemium; Cozi Gold $39/yr; ads in the free tier
competitors.note: The default 'family app' people already have. Not built for sitter handoff, but people improvise it with the shared lists. Since May 2024 free accounts see only a 30-day calendar window; Trustpilot averages ~2.1 stars; no data export; Common Sense Privacy rates it 'Warning' with data used for targeted advertising.

competitors.name: Touch Stay (and GoGuidebook, GuestIntro, Hostfully)
competitors.model: Subscription, ~$15/mo or ~$118/yr per guidebook; 14-day trial, no free tier
competitors.note: The closest premium analogue to what we are building: a digital guidebook you hand to someone via link and QR code, with deep links to specific sections. It explicitly markets a pet-sitter guidebook. Reviewers say the feature load is 'overwhelming if you just want a simple guidebook' — you pay for upsell widgets and analytics you never use.

competitors.name: Jotform / forms.app / Template.net online form builders
competitors.model: Free tier with an account; Jotform Starter = 5 forms, 100 submissions/mo, vendor branding; Silver $49/mo removes branding
competitors.note: forms.app publishes an actual 'Babysitter Information Sheet Template.' Works, but requires an account, stamps someone else's brand on your family's medical info, and the data sits on their servers — which is a genuinely bad fit for a document containing your address, alarm code, spare-key location, and your children's medications.

competitors.name: The Notes app, a text message, or a handwritten note on the fridge
competitors.note: The honest incumbent, and the one to actually beat. Zero friction and zero setup. Its failures are structural, not effort-based: nothing is in a predictable place, the sitter has to scroll a wall of text to find the allergy, and next month you start from scratch. We beat it on 'looks organized and reusable,' never on 'is faster to start.'

competitors.name: Printed babysitter notepads (e.g. MadGav 7x10 Babysitter Information Sheets, 120 pages)
competitors.note: Tear-off pad, one sheet per outing. Proves people will pay for the form factor. Same flaw as every paper option: no reuse of last time's answers, and your handwriting under time pressure is the readability spec.

complaints.complaint: Cozi's 2024 shift was called a 'bait and switch' — families who had used it for 8-10 years 'suddenly couldn't access their own data without paying.' Free accounts got clamped to a 30-day calendar window. Trustpilot sits around 2.1 stars.
complaints.source: usecalendara.com 'Cozi Review 2026: Honest Take After the Paywall'; ourcal.com Cozi review; Trustpilot aggregate cited in both
complaints.weWinIf: We never gate content the user typed. Say it on the page, not in a policy: 'Your sheet is stored on this device. There is no account to lose and nothing to renew.' The absence of a paywall is invisible unless we name it.

complaints.complaint: 'If you decide to leave Cozi, you can't take your data with you' — no CSV export, no calendar file download. Described as a significant lock-in concern.
complaints.weWinIf: Ship a one-tap 'Download my sheet' producing a plain JSON file plus the PDF, and an import that reads it back. Put the export button in the main UI, not buried in settings — it is a trust signal as much as a feature.

complaints.complaint: Cozi carries a Common Sense Privacy 'Warning' rating; user data is used for targeted advertising and the policy permits sharing with third parties. More broadly, Mozilla's reporting found the large majority of children's apps collect excessive personal data that is then sold to advertisers.
complaints.source: Common Sense Privacy rating cited in usecalendara review; Mozilla Foundation *Privacy Not Included reporting on children's apps and on false Google Play data-safety labels
complaints.weWinIf: Make 'nothing leaves your device' verifiable rather than claimed: zero network requests after load, and a line telling the user they can turn on airplane mode and the app still works. For a document containing a child's medications, home address, alarm code, and spare-key location, this is the single strongest thing we own.

complaints.complaint: Forced account creation on utility apps is now a leading cause of 1-star reviews: 'mandatory sign-up for utility apps,' 'no skip or use-without-account option,' 'login walls before the user has experienced any value.' Apple's own guideline 5.1.1 forbids requiring personal info that isn't core to functionality.
complaints.source: unstar.app 'App Privacy Complaints: What Users Say About Data Collection (2026)'; Apple App Review Guidelines 5.1.1 and the developer forum threads on registration-based rejections
complaints.weWinIf: No splash, no onboarding carousel, no template chooser. First paint is the first field with a cursor in it. Any interstitial we add is us reintroducing the exact thing users are one-starring competitors for.

complaints.complaint: Etsy digital-download buyers repeatedly report they 'can't download instantly,' can't get the PDF through the Etsy app, and that 'digital PDF files won't print.' Sellers note buyers leave negative reviews without ever asking for help.
complaints.source: Etsy Community Technical Issues forum threads: 'Customer Negative Reviews,' 'Digital PDF files won't print,' 'My clients have difficulties using the Etsy App to download my products'
complaints.weWinIf: Eliminate the download step entirely — the sheet exists in the browser and prints from there. Then earn the claim: ship a live print preview that IS the printed page, so nobody discovers a clipped column after they've already left the house.

complaints.complaint: Canva-based templates require a free Canva account before you can edit anything, and the delivery path is an email → a PDF of links → a browser editor. Multiple listings state the requirement outright as if it were a minor detail.
complaints.source: Etsy listing copy across babysitter/nanny binder templates ('You will need a free Canva account, but it only takes a couple of minutes')
complaints.weWinIf: Editing happens in place with no third party involved. Worth one line of marketing copy: 'No Canva account, no download, no email.'

complaints.complaint: Jotform's free tier caps you at 5 forms and 100 submissions a month, limits you to one user, and stamps Jotform branding on your form; removing the branding costs $49/mo on Silver.
complaints.source: Jotform Starter (Free) Plan Limits help page; Jotform pricing roundups (emitrr, formnx, costbench, verified Aug 2026)
complaints.weWinIf: Unlimited sheets, no submission concept at all, and no vendor branding on the printed page — or at most a small footer the user can switch off. A sheet that says someone else's brand name above your child's allergy list looks unserious to the sitter.

complaints.complaint: Touch Stay has no free tier at all (14-day trial only) at ~$15/mo or ~$118/yr per guidebook, and reviewers say 'the sheer number of features can be overwhelming if you just want a simple guidebook' — you pay for upsell widgets, analytics dashboards, and scheduled messaging you never touch.
complaints.source: guestintro.com 'Touch Stay vs Hostfully vs GuestIntro (2026)'; goguidebook.com comparison; G2 and Capterra Touch Stay pages
complaints.weWinIf: Give away the one thing they charge for — a QR/link that opens a clean read-only sitter page — and refuse the feature bloat. One page, one job, one screen of settings.

complaints.complaint: The stated failure mode of going digital-only: 'you could create a digital babysitting binder on a mobile phone or tablet, but if your battery gets completely drained then you lose access to all of your information.' Professional nanny guides still recommend a laminated quick-reference sheet alongside the digital copy.
complaints.source: kidsit.com 'Babysitting Binder'; seasidestaffingcompany.com 'Emergency Documents for Your Nanny: A Modern Safety Guide'
complaints.weWinIf: Treat print as a first-class output, not an escape hatch — it is why the app is called a Sheet. And make the shared sitter link cache offline on first open so a dead cell signal in someone else's basement doesn't erase the address.

complaints.complaint: The canonical checklists are enormous — 60 to 100 fields across ten categories (contacts, medical, fire safety, food, routine, house rules, household logistics, outing details, pets, digital access). kidsit's own advice, after listing all of it, is to 'condense everything into one or two pieces of paper.' Nobody completes this at 6:45pm with the sitter at the door.
complaints.source: kidsit.com 'What Info do you Leave for a Babysitter'; seasidestaffingcompany.com nanny emergency-documents guide
complaints.weWinIf: Progressive disclosure with a defined 'good enough' floor: six core fields produce a genuinely usable printed sheet, and everything else lives behind collapsed optional sections. Empty fields must never print — a half-filled sheet should look deliberate, not abandoned.

complaints.complaint: Sitters and nanny agencies keep flagging the same specific omissions: the wifi password (framed as an emergency tool, not a perk — 'the phone is the direct line to them'), allergies that were never gone over verbally, and no local backup contact within reach.
complaints.source: care.com 'Emergency contact info every babysitter and nanny needs'; sommetnannies.com; nannyquesthouseholdstaffing.com; seasidestaffingcompany.com
complaints.weWinIf: A completeness check that names the missing high-stakes fields specifically — 'No allergy info. No backup contact. No cross street.' — instead of a generic 87% progress ring. Nag about the four things that matter and stay silent about the other sixty.

complaints.complaint: Every professional guide requires written authorization for emergency medical treatment plus insurance card details, and no free one-page printable bundles that onto the same sheet — it's a separate form in a separate binder, which is why it's the piece most often missing when it matters.
complaints.source: seasidestaffingcompany.com ('Written permission for emergency medical treatment'); kidsit.com ('Healthcare authorization form', photocopy of insurance card)
complaints.weWinIf: An optional consent-to-treat block with a signature line, printed date, insurer and member ID, and preferred hospital — on the same page, off by default. It costs us one collapsed section and closes a gap the free printables structurally can't.

tableStakes: Per-child sections, not one flat form. Allergies, meds, bedtime, and comfort items differ per kid; every credible printable splits them. A single set of fields for 'the children' reads instantly amateur to a parent of two.

It remembers. The whole reason to use an app instead of the free PDF is that next month you edit last month's sheet instead of rewriting it. Show an 'Updated [date]' stamp on the printed page so the sitter knows it isn't stale.

Print output that is actually one page: empty fields dropped, columns that don't clip, no browser header/footer URL garbage, real black on white. This is the make-or-break, and it is exactly where the PDF competitors visibly fail.
Save as PDF / produce a file. Most parents no longer own a printer; if the only success path ends at a printer tray, the app fails for a large share of users on their first try.
Copy as plain text that pastes cleanly into SMS or WhatsApp. Universally compatible, needs nothing installed on the sitter's phone, and survives a 15-year-old's cracked Android.

Tap-to-call on every phone number in the sitter's view, with 911 and Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) always present and not removable. Poison Control appears in essentially every professional checklist; its absence is noticed.
Home address with nearest cross street, formatted to be read aloud to a 911 dispatcher. Both professional guides call this out separately from the address field.

A separate read-only sitter view. The parent's edit form and the sitter's reference page are different documents with different layouts — shipping only the form and calling it done is the tell of an unfinished app.

The expected field taxonomy present somewhere, even if collapsed: contacts (parent, partner, 2+ local backups, one out-of-state), medical (allergies, meds with dosage, conditions, pediatrician, insurance, preferred hospital), routine (meals, nap, full bedtime sequence), house rules (screen time, off-limits rooms, guests, discipline, no-posting-photos), logistics (wifi, alarm code, spare key, thermostat, where things live), pets, and 'where we are + when we're back.'

Multiple saved sheets or modes — babysitter vs pet sitter vs grandparent weekend — each with its own stored answers. The current build already splits babysitter/pet; the pattern needs to extend to named sheets.
differentiators: Ninety seconds to a usable sheet. Six core fields — kids + allergies, parent cell, one local backup, address + cross street, bedtime, wifi — produce a genuinely printable page on their own. Everything else is collapsed behind 'Add more.' Beat the printables on time-to-done, not on field count.
Both outputs free, from one form: the fridge print and a QR/link that opens a read-only, tap-to-call sitter page. Touch Stay charges ~$118/yr for essentially the second half of that.

A '3-second panel' pinned to the top of the sitter view and the top of the print: street address + cross street, allergies, and 911 / Poison Control as tap-to-call. Always rendered at maximum size even if the parent filled in nothing else. Design for the worst three seconds this document will ever have.

Allergies and medications auto-promoted. Whatever the parent types into those two fields renders as the loudest element on both outputs, with a red chip. The parent cannot accidentally bury the thing that matters most in a wall of house rules.

A live print preview that is literally the printed page, advertised as a feature: 'One page. Nothing cut off. No printer required.' The loudest complaint against the printable competitors is that the PDF wouldn't print right — we can make that our headline.
The no-printer path as three equal buttons, never a menu: Print, Copy as text, QR for the sitter's phone. Half the audience has no printer and finds out at 6:45pm.

Optional consent-to-treat + insurance block on the same sheet — signature line, date, insurer, member ID, preferred hospital. Every nanny agency demands it; no free one-pager includes it. The portfolio already ships a signature-maker to lean on.
Export the whole thing as a file the user owns, with a visible button. Direct, nameable answer to Cozi's 'you can't take your data with you' — and the proof behind our no-account claim.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: Two visual worlds collide here. (1) The printable/Etsy world that currently owns the search results: script and serif display fonts, watercolor florals, 'boho neutral' beige-sage-and-cream, hand-drawn icons, and a decorative header that eats the top third of the page. Beautiful on Pinterest, close to useless at arm's length in a dim hallway. (2) The app world: 2026 parenting apps have converged on cleaner layouts, modern typography, streamlined dashboards, and warm secondary palettes — yellow, orange, green — chosen for friendliness, with button roundness and illustration tone deliberately tuned to the parent's emotional state (Fireart's parenting-app redesign case study, FamilyTime's 2026 parent-app redesign). Clearly dated: rainbow-crayon 'kid-coded' chrome and Comic Sans; baby-blue/baby-pink gendering; glossy skeuomorphic buttons and iOS-6 gradients; clipart babies; and the dense grey Excel grid. Also to be avoided despite trend lists naming it: neumorphism / soft-UI, whose low contrast fails outright for this use case.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: One document, two readers, two very different states. THE PARENT fills it in the last ten minutes before leaving — half-dressed, kid on hip, sitter already at the door — while carrying real low-grade anxiety and guilt. The parenting literature is consistent that this is normal and near-universal ('worry, and guilt for even thinking about leaving baby'; 'perfectly natural to feel nervous the first time'). That parent will abandon anything that feels like homework, so entry must be resumable, forgiving, and must look complete at 40% filled. THE SITTER reads it standing up in a stranger's house, in bad hallway light, often a fifteen-year-old on a cracked phone or a grandparent without reading glasses, sometimes one-handed over a crying child — and occasionally in a genuine emergency where the address and the allergy need to be found in under three seconds. That second reader, not the first, sets the type spec. Concretely: sitter-view body type floors around 18-19px with phone numbers at 22px+ in 48px tap targets; allergy and medication lines rendered as the loudest thing on the page no matter how casually the parent typed them; address plus cross street in a fixed, always-visible block; print at 11-12pt minimum in true black on white, never grey-on-grey; generous line height because the reading posture is standing and glancing, not sitting and studying. And the overall temperature should be warm rather than clinical — a nervous parent should not feel they are completing a hospital intake form about their own child.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: warm, calm, grown-up, plainspoken, reassuring, legible-first

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Dusk plum / aubergine — a desaturated red-violet. Suggested light-mode accent around #6D3A5D (contrast on white ≈ 8.7:1, comfortably AA for body text, not just large type), lifting to roughly #D9A0C0 for dark mode. Fallback if plum reads too close to its neighbors in the hub grid: a yellow-green sage-olive around #5C6B3C (≈5.8:1 on white), distinct from Sub Plans' blue-green forest and reading homey-kitchen rather than clinical.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Emotionally it is the color of the hour the app is used — early evening, the handoff at the door, date night. Warm and calm without being nursery-cute, grown-up enough that a parent doesn't feel infantilised while entering their child's medications. Functionally it keeps red completely free as a pure signal: this sheet contains allergies, dosages, 911 and Poison Control, and red must mean danger and nothing else, so the brand hue cannot be red or amber. Portfolio-wise it fills a genuinely empty lane. Across the 23 apps, five already run blue (#2563eb, #1d4ed8, #3b82f6), four run teal (#0f766e), four run blue-violet (#7c3aed), and three run amber (#b45309) — including Sitter Sheet's current accent, which collides directly with Bracket Maker and Moving Boxes. Plum separates cleanly from all three near neighbours: from Wedding Timeline's #7c3aed by being red-shifted and far lower in chroma, from Wheel Picker's #be185d by being darker and desaturated, and from Secret Santa's #b91c1c by being violet rather than red.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Blue in any form — five apps already own it, and it makes this read like a corporate intake form or an insurance PDF, exactly the tone that makes an anxious parent close the tab. Violet #7c3aed specifically — Baby Log already owns it and Baby Log is the nearest neighbour in the same parenting category; the two icons will be confused in the hub grid. Red, crimson, or amber as the brand hue — the sheet's entire job is that the allergy, medication, and emergency lines out-shout everything else, and if the chrome is warm-red the warnings have nowhere left to go; reserve red exclusively for the allergy chip and the 911 / Poison Control row. Pastel baby-blue and baby-pink, and the Etsy 'boho beige + sage + script' palette — gendered, low-contrast, and the visual signature of the free printables we are trying to beat. Pure greyscale or slate — Caregiver Log and Pill Schedule already use #57606d, and grey reads institutional and medical here, which amplifies parental anxiety rather than settling it. And anything low-contrast (neumorphism, soft-UI, tinted-grey body text), which fails outright in hallway light on a sitter's phone.

confidence:
HIGH on competitor structure and pricing, which came from primary or well-corroborated pages: Cozi Gold $39/yr with a 30-day free calendar window since May 2024; Touch Stay at ~$15/mo, ~$118/yr, 14-day trial, no free tier; Jotform Starter at 5 forms / 100 submissions per month / 1 user / vendor branding, $49/mo Silver to remove it. HIGH on the field taxonomy — two independent professional sources (kidsit.com's parent checklist and Seaside Staffing's nanny emergency-documents guide) were fetched in full and agree closely, and the ten-category structure in the Table Stakes section is drawn from them directly. HIGH on the structural finding that no dedicated app owns this niche: every 'babysitter app' surfaced in both stores is a sitter *marketplace* (Care.com, UrbanSitter, Sitly, Babysits, Kiddocare, SitterTree), and the info-sheet job is served by printables, form builders, and paid guidebook SaaS.

MEDIUM on complaint texture, and here is what I could not verify. Reddit is not fetchable by this agent — WebSearch rejects reddit.com outright — so I have no first-hand Reddit threads despite the brief asking for them; treat the absence of Reddit quotes as a tooling limit, not evidence that the gripes don't exist there. Trustpilot and JustUseApp both returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so the Cozi user language ('bait and switch', 'you can't take your data with you', the 2.1-star Trustpilot average, the Common Sense Privacy 'Warning' rating) is reported second-hand via the usecalendara and ourcal 2026 reviews rather than read from the original review pages — reliable as reporting, but I did not see the raw reviews. Same for unstar.app's forced-signup review language (403), which I have only through the search snippet, though Apple's guideline 5.1.1 independently corroborates the underlying pattern.

COULD NOT VERIFY: any 1-3 star review text for a dedicated babysitter-info-sheet app, because no such app exists at scale to review — which is itself the most important finding in this report. The Mozilla figure on children's apps collecting excessive data came through a secondary summary rather than a Mozilla page I fetched, so cite it loosely or not at all. My searches for Canva-template and no-printer complaints in parents' own words returned product pages rather than user sentiment; the Etsy download-and-print complaints I did land come from Etsy's seller forum (sellers describing buyer behaviour) rather than from buyers directly.

AESTHETIC claims about 2026 parenting-app direction come from design-studio case studies and trend roundups — directional, not survey data. The portfolio colour audit is first-hand: I read the accent tokens out of all 23 apps' index.html files, so the collision counts and the note that Sitter Sheet currently ships #b45309 (shared with Bracket Maker and Moving Boxes) are exact. The contrast ratios are my own WCAG calculations, not measured in the running app.
